name: Cubism
summary: A picture that shows an object from several sides at once. Analytic Cubism breaks the subject into faceted planes in a narrow brown-grey key; Synthetic Cubism rebuilds it from flat shapes, pasted paper and brighter colour.

philosophy.core_thesis: A picture is an object in its own right, and it shows what a thing is by combining several viewpoints on one flat surface.
design_principles: Break the subject into 20–60 planes with mostly straight edges, and show each plane from a different viewpoint.
Keep the space shallow: stack planes in 2–4 layers that lean forward and never open a deep perspective.
In the analytic phase, limit the palette to 3–4 hues of ochre, grey, brown and olive.
Make the contour pass through the form: let edges open, so that figure and ground exchange places.
Set a grid of verticals and horizontals as the armature, and tilt the planes 5–20° from it.
In the synthetic phase, use flat shapes in solid colour, and add real texture: pasted paper, sand, a stencilled letter.
Choose a plain, close subject that stands on a table: a guitar, a bottle, a glass, a newspaper, a head.
anti_patterns: Deep single-point perspective with a receding floor
Smooth modelling that turns a form as one solid volume
Soft atmospheric edges and blended colour
A single viewpoint and a full, undistorted face
Strong cast shadows from one light source
Sentimental or narrative subjects that need a story

composition.layout: A central, pyramidal mass of faceted planes that fades out toward the edges, on a hidden grid of verticals and horizontals with the planes tilted 5–20° off it.
composition.focal_point: The densest cluster of small planes and the strongest value contrast, within the centre 40% of the canvas.
composition.format: A vertical canvas of 4:5 to 2:3, or an oval; the subject floats inside with a 10–15% margin of lighter ground.

principles.rule: Repeat the same angled facet 10–20 times, with each repeat shifted or rotated by 5–20°.
Compress depth to 2–4 shallow planes with no more than 10% value change between neighbours.
Concentrate detail and contrast at the centre; let the facets thin out toward the edges.
Hold the key to 3–4 hues and one value range; vary the facet size from 10 to 100mm.
Balance the mass by an informal offset: a heavy cluster left of centre against open facets on the right.

palette.strategy: Analytic: a near-monochrome of ochre, grey and brown. Synthetic: flat, brighter local colour, with black, white and one or two primaries.
palette.distribution: Analytic: one hue family 80–90%, near-white highlights 5–10%, near-black lines under 5%. Synthetic: 4–6 flat colours, each 10–25% of the area.
palette.ground: A pale ochre or warm grey ground that shows between the planes.

brushwork_and_medium.medium: Oil paint, thinly bound; later with sand, wallpaper, newsprint and charcoal.
brushwork_and_medium.support: Canvas, medium weave, with a pale ground.
brushwork_and_medium.brushwork: Small, flat strokes of 5–15mm laid in parallel within each plane, and directed along the facet; a tiny, dabbed 'passage' at plane joins.
brushwork_and_medium.paint_handling: Thin, dry and matt in the analytic phase; flat, opaque fields with sanded or collaged areas in the synthetic phase.
brushwork_and_medium.edges: Alternating hard and lost edges along the same contour, so that a plane breaks into its neighbour (passage).

light_and_modelling.light: No single source; light is a pattern of lighter and darker planes spread over the whole object.
light_and_modelling.modelling: Each plane has a flat or lightly graded value, 2–3 steps; the solid form is implied by the sequence of planes.
light_and_modelling.shadow: Shadow is a dark plane in its own right, not a cast shadow; the darkest value stays inside the figure.
light_and_modelling.temperature: One warm-earth family in the analytic phase; in the synthetic phase, warm and cool are set by flat fields side by side.

subject.typical: Still life with guitar, violin, bottle and newspaper; heads and half-figures; café tables; a few landscapes.
subject.figure_scale: The subject fills 60–85% of the canvas and is seen close.
subject.treatment: Everyday, unheroic objects; an exact likeness is lost, and the identity is kept by a few clues such as a sound-hole, a letter or a scroll.

surface.finish: Matt and dry; sometimes a gloss field against matt planes.
surface.texture: Flat canvas grain, with sand, paper edge or wood-grain print in the synthetic phase.

reference_works.note: These works are not flagged as public domain by the museum. The ids identify the works only. Look at the museum page for the image and its licence; do not copy it.

emotion.target_response: Intellectual alertness: the viewer reads the picture as a puzzle and sees one object from several sides.

use_cases: portrait illustration with a modern edge
avoid_when: The brief needs a clear, friendly face or a recognisable likeness at a glance.
The subject needs a soft, warm or calm mood.

modifiers.how: Keep the flat planes and the grid; reduce the shapes to rectangles, set a primary palette with black bars, and drop the object.
Keep the shallow space; make the planes loose and large, show each stroke of 50–150mm, and drop the subject entirely.
